grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Uma bolsa → a bolsa. Um livro → o livro. A bolsa é azul; o livro não é de Ana.

rows: O livro não é de Ana.

grammar.note_en:
Portuguese nouns have grammatical gender: masculine or feminine. This is a word’s grammatical class, not the sex of the object. Learn a noun with its article: um livro means “a book,” and uma bolsa means “a bag.” O livro and a bolsa mean “the book” and “the bag.” The definite article o/a points to something identified in the scene; um/uma introduces one instance. Both sets here are singular, referring to one thing. We will meet plurals later.

An adjective describes a noun. It normally follows it here: a bolsa azul, “the blue bag”; o livro preto, “the black book.” Some adjectives change with gender: aberto/aberta means “open,” and fechado/fechada means “closed.” Grande (“large”) and azul (“blue”) have the same singular form with either gender. A bag’s blue color alone does not establish its owner.

É, está and tem are different verb forms. A bolsa é azul means “The bag is blue”: é describes or identifies. O livro está aqui means “The book is here”: está locates it. A bolsa tem um livro means “The bag has/contains a book”: tem gives its contents. The difference between ser and estar is not simply permanent versus temporary. Here, learn these particular uses; later contexts extend them. Não comes before the verb to negate it: O livro não é de Ana, “The book is not Ana’s.” Paulo não está aqui means “Paulo is not here.”

De links an owner to a thing: o livro de Bia, “Bia’s book.” Em gives a location: em uma mesa, “on a table.” Portuguese em can correspond to English “in” or “on”; the actual object and scene tell you which relationship is meant. Com means “with”: Ana está com a chave, “Ana has/is holding the key.” E joins information (“and”); mas introduces a contrast (“but”). Aqui means “here,” the place currently being pointed out.

Pega means “takes/holds,” vê means “sees,” and abre means “opens.” These are the forms used with one named person. We are learning these action frames, not entire conjugations. Quem asks “who”: Quem tem a bolsa? means “Who has the bag?” Onde asks “where”: Onde está o livro? means “Where is the book?” An answer can omit a subject already clear from the question: Não está aqui, “It is not here.” Ask about the story rather than guessing from color alone. A name on a book is evidence about that object; the characters compare the separate evidence before treating the whole bag as another person’s.

Estar also describes a condition in this chapter: A porta está fechada means “The door is closed,” and O livro está aberto means “The book is open.” These are the particular state words met here, not a rule that every adjective must follow estar. The table also gives A bolsa tem um livro, “The bag contains a book”; A chave tem um nome, “The key has a name”; and O livro não é de Ana, “The book is not Ana’s.” The article rows mean “a book → the book,” “a bag → the bag,” “a sheet of paper → the sheet of paper,” and “a key → the key.”
